sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Botensilimab (BOT) is a fragment crystallizable (Fc)-enhanced multifunctional anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) antibody with differentiated mechanisms of action, designed to extend therapy to cold/poorly immunogenic solid tumors. Patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) who progress on or after first-line immunotherapy have limited treatment options. Here, we report findings from a phase 1b study of BOT plus balstilimab (BAL; anti-programmed cell death protein 1 [PD-1] antibody) in previously treated patients with HCC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This is an open-label, nonrandomized, phase 1b, multicenter study of BOT±BAL in patients with advanced solid tumors. The study began with dose escalation (3 + 3 design) then dose expansion with multiple disease-specific cohorts. An expanded cohort of 19 patients with HCC who progressed on or after prior immunotherapy (primarily atezolizumab/bevacizumab) are included in this analysis. Patients with HCC received BOT intravenously at 1 or 2 mg/kg once every 6 weeks for up to 2 years plus BAL intravenously 3 mg/kg once every 2 weeks, for up to 2 years. Endpoints included safety, objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate, duration of response, and progression-free survival (PFS). Overall survival (OS) was an exploratory endpoint.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 18 efficacy evaluable patients (with ≥1 post-baseline 6-week imaging scan), ORR was 17% (3/18; 95% CI: 4–41), and 18-week clinical benefit rate (a complete or partial response or stable disease) 50% (9/18; 95% CI: 26–74). Median PFS was 4.4 months (95% CI: 1.4–6.9), and median OS was 12.3 months (95% CI: 8.4–21.4). Thirteen patients (68%) experienced any-grade immune-mediated treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs), with 37% (7/19) grade 3. The most common immune-mediated TRAEs included diarrhea/colitis (37% [7/19]; 16% grade 3 [3/19]), hepatitis (21% [4/19]; 16% grade 3 [3/19]), and dermatologic events (21% [4/19]; 5% grade 3 [1/19]). There were no treatment-related deaths or new safety signals outside of the class.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The BOT+BAL combination demonstrated durable responses and manageable safety in treatment-refractory patients with HCC previously treated with immunotherapy, supporting further investigation in randomized studies. Despite the small sample size and high percentage of patients with albumin-bilirubin grade 2 liver disease, these results provide early evidence of antitumor activity in a difficult-to-treat disease setting.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In the past 5 years, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the management of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Atezolizumab/bevacizumab and durvalumab/tremelimumab are both approved first-line regimens based on superior overall survival (OS) compared to sorafenib [1, 2]. More recently, nivolumab/ipilimumab resulted in improved OS compared with sorafenib or lenvatinib, gaining FDA approval [3]. While these regimens have benefited patients, a significant challenge exists in second-line treatment and beyond [1–4]. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as sorafenib, lenvatinib, cabozantinib, and regorafenib are used post-ICI therapy based on real-world evidence or single-arm phase 2 trials, with modest outcomes [5–8]. An unmet need exists for the development of novel therapeutics for patients with HCC who have been treated with ICIs in the first line.

Botensilimab (BOT) is a multifunctional anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 (CTLA-4) antibody designed with an enhanced IgG1 fragment crystallizable (Fc) region, providing stronger Fc gamma receptor (FcγR)-binding capabilities than traditional CTLA-4 inhibitors [9]. These enhancements facilitate more effective interactions between T cells, antigen presenting cells, and natural killer cells, leading to enhanced T-cell priming, memory, and activation, and myeloid stimulation [9, 10]. BOT also reduces intratumoral regulatory T-cell populations through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and phagocytosis mechanisms [9]. Additionally, point mutation in the Fc region aids in mitigating complement-mediated toxicities associated with conventional anti-CTLA-4 therapy [9]. Balstilimab (BAL) is a fully human monoclonal antibody that binds to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), blocking its interaction with programmed cell death ligand 1/2. BAL enhances T-cell activation and effector function with pharmacological effectiveness comparable to currently approved PD-1 inhibitors [11, 12]. Recent results from a phase 1b, open-label study of BOT±BAL have shown promising outcomes in poorly immunogenic/treatment-refractory solid tumors including some ICI-refractory tumors [9, 13–17].

Here, we report the results of BOT+BAL in an expansion cohort of patients with previously treated HCC, conducted as part of the previously reported phase 1b trial of BOT±BAL in solid tumors [9, 14–17].

sec.title: Study Design and Patients
sec.p: The C-800-01 study is an open-label, nonrandomized, phase 1b, multicenter study evaluating the safety, tolerability, and efficacy of BOT±BAL (NCT03860272). Patients with HCC were enrolled from March 25, 2021, to September 27, 2023, at 6 US sites (1 patient during dose escalation; 18 patients during dose expansion; online suppl. Fig. 1 and online suppl. Methods; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000551630).

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: BOT was administered intravenously at 1 or 2 mg/kg once every 6 weeks for up to 2 years plus BAL intravenously 3 mg/kg once every 2 weeks, for up to 2 years. The treatment algorithm for the management of immune-mediated diarrhea/colitis with BOT+BAL has been described previously [16]. Use of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) inhibitors (i.e., infliximab) for immune-mediated treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) was restricted to the management of immune-mediated diarrhea/colitis.

sec.title: Endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the occurrence of dose-limiting toxicities in the dose escalation period. The full study design, dose escalation, and results from other cohorts have been previously reported [14–16]. A maximum tolerated dose was not reached in the C-800-01 phase 1b trial, and BOT doses up to 2 mg/kg were considered safe [14]. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), and progression-free survival (PFS), all investigator-assessed per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST 1.1). Imaging was performed every 6 weeks (±3 days) from the first treatment dose to 1 year after and then every 12 weeks (±7 days) thereafter. OS was included as an exploratory endpoint. Clinical benefit rate (CBR) was defined as stable disease or better for ≥18 weeks. Details regarding efficacy outcomes with prior therapies were not collected. Immune-mediated TRAEs were defined as related to treatment with the patient receiving steroids and/or immunosuppressants or endocrine replacement for any reason during the event and were comprised of multiple preferred terms.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The data cutoff date was December 5, 2024. The safety analysis set included all patients who received ≥1 dose of study drug (n = 19). The efficacy evaluable set included patients who had ≥1 post-baseline 6-week imaging scan (n = 18).

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p: Nineteen patients were enrolled with a median age of 67 years (range, 39–82) and a median of 2 prior lines of therapy (range, 1–7) (Table 1). All patients received prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy (100%), 13 patients (68%) had prior TKIs, and 11 patients (58%) had prior atezolizumab/bevacizumab. One patient (5%) received prior CTLA-4 therapy. Nine patients (47%) received 1 mg/kg BOT, while 10 received the 2 mg/kg dose of BOT (53%). Nine patients (47%) had an albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score of 2, 13 (68%) had extrahepatic metastases, and 9 (n = 9/17 with baseline data; 53%) had an alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level >400 ng/mL.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: ORR was 17% (3/18; 95% CI: 4–41), including 1 complete and 2 partial responses, while CBR was 50% (9/18; 95% CI: 26–74) (Fig. 1; online suppl. Table 1). Median DOR was not reached (NR; 95% CI: 9.8–NR). Median PFS was 4.4 months (95% CI: 1.4–6.9), and median OS was 12.3 months (95% CI: 8.4–21.4) (online suppl. Fig. 2), with a median follow-up of 11.4 months (range, 1.5–34.3). All 3 responders received prior atezolizumab/bevacizumab; 1 also received lenvatinib; another also received sorafenib and a MER/AXL-targeted therapy via a clinical trial. As demonstrated by the CBR, benefit with BOT+BAL was not confined to RECIST 1.1, and 1 patient had stable disease for 66 weeks.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The safety profile of BOT+BAL was consistent with previous reports. No dose-limiting toxicities occurred with BOT+BAL in this HCC cohort. There were no treatment-related deaths or new class safety signals. TRAEs occurred in all patients (100%), with grade ≥3 in 11 patients (58%) (online suppl. Table 2). The most common any-grade TRAEs included diarrhea/colitis in 9 patients (47%; 16% grade 3 [3/19]) and fatigue in 8 patients (42%; no grade ≥3 events). Nine patients (47%) discontinued any study drug due to a TRAE. No treatment-related deaths were observed (no grade 5 TRAEs).

Immune-mediated TRAEs were defined as related to treatment with the patient receiving steroids and/or immunosuppressants or endocrine replacement for any reason during the event (Table 2; analyzed using grouped terms defined in the table footnote). Thirteen patients (68%) experienced any immune-mediated TRAEs (37% grade 3 [7/19]), most commonly diarrhea/colitis in 7 patients (37%; 16% grade 3 [3/19]), hepatitis in 4 patients (21%; 16% grade 3 [3/19]), and dermatologic events in 4 patients (21%; 5% grade 3 [1/19]). When analyzed as a single, preferred term, 1 patient (5%) experienced immune-mediated hepatitis (grade 3) (online suppl. Table 3). There were no grade ≥4 immune-mediated TRAEs. Seven patients (37%) permanently discontinued any study drug due to an immune-mediated TRAE (online suppl. Table 4).

sec.p: Twelve patients (63%) received systemic steroids and/or TNF-α inhibitors, while 3 (16%) received hormone replacement for an immune-mediated adverse event. Four patients experienced immune-mediated hepatitis and all events resolved to grade ≤1 (managed with steroids alone). Seven patients had a total of 16 immune-mediated diarrhea/colitis events, all treated with steroids and/or TNF-α inhibitors, with nearly all resolving completely (15/16; 94%).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase 1b cohort of patients with treatment-refractory HCC and prior exposure to ICI-based therapy, BOT+BAL demonstrated durable responses with an ORR of 17%, prolonged disease control (18-week CBR of 50%), a median DOR that was not reached (95% CI: 9.8 months to NR), and a median OS of 12.3 months. All patients had prior anti-PD-(L)1 therapy, many had received TKIs (68%) and/or atezolizumab/bevacizumab (58%), and nearly half (47%) had ALBI 2 liver function, collectively representing a heavily pretreated population with limited prospective data and typically reduced responsiveness to subsequent therapy. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a prospective cohort of patients with HCC treated with combined CTLA-4/PD-1 inhibition (BOT+BAL) after front-line ICI exposure.

While the first-line treatment of advanced HCC has been revolutionized with the advent of anti-PD-(L)1-based combinations, the management of patients with advanced HCC after ICI-based first-line therapy remains largely empiric and guided by data generated in the era of sorafenib as first-line therapy, along with real-world evidence, retrospective series, and single-arm phase 2 trials [18–23]. Additionally, across many of these studies, eligibility criteria have frequently favored patients with preserved liver function, and reporting of ALBI score distributions has been inconsistent. This is of importance, as the ALBI 2 score has been associated with a 4- to 10-month decrement in median OS compared with ALBI 1 in HCC studies [21, 24]. Accordingly, cross-trial comparisons are limited by the exploratory design and broad inclusion criteria of the current study, which included patients with ALBI 2 liver function (47%) and other high-risk features associated with poor prognosis, including extrahepatic metastases (68%) and AFP levels >400 ng/mL (53%) [25–27].

Within this context, currently available post-ICI systemic therapies have shown limited activity, with prior studies highlighting the modest effectiveness of available options in the post-ICI setting. Lenvatinib, cabozantinib, and regorafenib have all been evaluated in phase 2 studies following ICI-based therapy and demonstrated ORRs of 6–14%, median PFS of approximately 4–5 months, and median OS of ≤10.5 months [21–23]. In a phase 2 study of regorafenib plus pembrolizumab after prior ICI therapy (multiple cohorts based on prior ICI regimen), ORR (6–11%) and PFS (3–4 months) were comparable to those observed with single-agent regorafenib [7, 8, 28]. Retrospective evaluations of first-generation anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-(L)1 combinations after prior ICI exposure are similarly constrained by small sample sizes, heterogeneous first-line therapies (including patients who received single-agent anti-PD-[L]1 therapy in first line), and selection bias toward patients with Child-Pugh A liver function [18–20]. In these retrospective cohorts, nivolumab plus ipilimumab has demonstrated ORRs of 13–22% and a median OS of 7–12 months [18–20]. Taken together, within the limitations of this exploratory small prospective cohort and cross-study comparisons, the ORR, median DOR, and survival observed with BOT+BAL in the post-ICI setting are numerically favorable relative to TKIs and within the range reported for first-generation anti-CTLA-4 plus PD-(L)1 combinations in retrospective series, which (unlike this study) frequently selected patients with preserved liver function.

The findings with BOT+BAL in this cohort highlight a potentially differentiated activity profile that warrants further investigation. Together with previous reports, these findings suggest that BOT's enhanced Fc engagement and multifunctional activity may overcome resistance mechanisms to conventional ICI [9, 10, 13–17]. Unlike traditional CTLA-4 inhibitors, BOT leverages distinct FcγR-dependent mechanisms to transform “cold” immune-excluded tumor microenvironments into “hot” immune responsive ones by enhancing T-cell priming, activation, and memory, stimulating myeloid activation, and promoting more effective depletion of intratumoral regulatory T cells. These mechanisms have been characterized across previously published studies [9, 10].

The safety profile was manageable and consistent with other disease cohorts treated with BOT+BAL, with immune-mediated TRAEs such as diarrhea/colitis being the most common (any grade, 37%; grade 3, 16%) but largely reversible with appropriate management including steroid and/or infliximab use. No grade ≥4 immune-mediated TRAEs were reported, and grade 3 events occurred in 7 patients (37%). By comparison, previously published anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-(L)1 studies in HCC reported consolidated grade 3–4 immune-mediated adverse event rates of 13–28% in patients who were naïve to any prior systemic therapy [2, 3].

Notably, immune-mediated hepatitis is a recognized toxicity of ICIs, particularly in HCC, where underlying liver dysfunction, variability in adverse event definitions, and attributions by investigators contribute to a wide range of reported rates [29]. In previous studies, grade 3–4 “immune-mediated hepatitis” analyzed using various approaches (i.e., tabulated using single preferred terms or multiple grouped terms) has been observed in 2–20% of patients receiving other anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-(L)1-based regimens [3, 19, 29, 30]. In this small cohort with a high proportion of patients with ALBI 2 scores, TRAEs of immune-mediated hepatitis (analyzed by grouped terms that included aspartate aminotransferase increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, immune-mediated hepatitis, blood bilirubin increased, and hepatic enzyme increased) occurred in 21% (n = 4) of patients, with 16% (n = 3) experiencing grade 3 events and no grade ≥4 events; all of which resolved to grade ≤1. The single term, “immune-mediated hepatitis” was reported in 1 patient (5%, grade 3) in this cohort. Within these clinical constraints, the incidence of high-grade immune-mediated events observed with BOT+BAL supports a tolerability profile consistent with other anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-(L)1-based regimens in advanced HCC.

Among the 9 patients (47%) who discontinued BOT+BAL due to a TRAE, 7 (37%) did so due to an immune-mediated TRAE. Prior studies with ICIs indicate that the development of immune-mediated adverse events, even at higher grades, is associated with improved clinical outcomes, and patients who discontinue treatment can still experience durable responses [31–33]. Findings with BOT+BAL in the pan-tumor setting (n = 339) have also demonstrated this, with an additional 10 months of median OS observed among patients who experienced immune-mediated TRAEs compared to those who did not [17]. Therefore, although discontinuations appeared frequent in this cohort, prior evidence suggests that immune-mediated TRAEs do not imply reduced efficacy and may accompany sustained disease control.

This small, exploratory expansion cohort study without biomarker evaluation has several limitations. Given the small number of patients, findings regarding efficacy and safety in this cohort should be interpreted with caution. The eligibility criteria did not initially require Child-Pugh A liver function. A high percentage of patients had an ALBI score of 2, which is associated with a poorer prognosis. Further, the size and composition of this cohort did not support the ability to study liver function-based dose adjustment, which could be an area of future study in this disease state. We did not collect information about outcome and duration of treatment on first-line ICI-based therapy, which may also influence the outcomes observed with BOT+BAL and limit the ability to assess patterns of ICI resistance. Subgroup analyses by line of therapy were not performed for this small exploratory cohort. Future studies should also explore predictive markers of response, including immune infiltration characteristics and alterations in FcγR pathway components that may be uniquely relevant to the mechanism of action of BOT. Of note, predictive markers of response with BOT+BAL have been studied across other larger patient cohorts from the C-800-01 study in colorectal, sarcoma, and ovarian cancer [14–16].

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: BOT+BAL demonstrated promising efficacy and manageable safety in patients with previously treated HCC, including those who progressed after front-line ICI. This encouraging activity in a patient population with a significant unmet need warrants further investigation.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: The data that support the findings of this study are not publicly available due to privacy reasons. De-identified data are available upon reasonable request by a qualified investigator for academic use (subject to the constraints of the informed consent provided). Researchers interested in accessing these data can submit a request, along with a signed data transfer agreement, to the corresponding author (Anthony B. El-Khoueiry; elkhouei@usc.edu). Access will be granted to those who agree to the terms outlined in the data transfer agreement, which include using the data solely for research purposes and ensuring the confidentiality of patient and data information for the duration of the agreement. The data will be accessible for requests up to 2 years following the conclusion of the C-800-01 study. Each request will be reviewed individually, with responses provided within a maximum of 2 weeks. Further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author.
